The second: the whole day. This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: its heat. This is the view of al-Suddi and Muqatil.

﴿And the moon when it follows it﴾. Regarding this, there are two opinions.

(p-138) The first: when it follows it. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and others. Then, concerning the time of its following it, there are three opinions. The first: that it is on the first night of the month, when the moon is seen as the sun sets, as Qatadah said. The second: that it is on the fifteenth, when the moon rises together with the setting of the sun, as related by al-Mawardi. The third: that it is in the first half of the month, when the sun sets and the moon follows it in brightness and is behind it in light, as related by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

The second opinion: when it aligns with it. This is the view of Mujahid. Others said: when it becomes full, so that it follows the sun in radiance and light, and this is on the bright nights.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the day when it reveals it﴾. Regarding the referent of the pronoun "it" (hā), there are two opinions.

The first: that it refers to the sun. This is the view of Mujahid, so the meaning is: "and the day when it makes the sun clear," because the sun becomes manifest when the day spreads out.

The second: that it refers to the darkness, so it is a pronoun referring to something not mentioned, because the meaning is known, as you say: "It became cold," and "the wind blew from the north." This is the view of al-Farra' and the linguists.

﴿And the night when it covers it﴾, that is, it covers the sun when it sets, so the horizons become dark.

(p-139) The first: that it means "man" (who), with the sense "and He who built it." This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid and Abu Ubaydah. Some take it to mean "alladhī" (who).

The second: that it is a verbal noun, meaning "and its building." This is the view of Qatadah and al-Zajjaj. The same applies to ﴿and He who spread it out﴾ and ﴿and He who fashioned it﴾. Abu Imran al-Jawni and others recited "wa-man banāhā," "wa-man ṭaḥāhā," and "wa-man sawwāhā," all with the letter nūn. Abu Ubaydah said: the meaning of "ṭaḥāhā" is that He spread it out to the right and left and from every side. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said "khayrun ṭāḥin," meaning abundant and wide.

Regarding the meaning of "the soul" (nafs) here, there are two opinions.

The first: Adam, as said by al-Hasan.

The second: all souls, as said by Ata'. We have already explained the meaning of "sawwāhā" in (p-140) the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He fashioned you and made you balanced﴾ [al-Infitar: 7].

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He made it bound to its wickedness and its righteousness. Ibn Zayd said: He placed this in it, by granting it success toward righteousness and forsaking it toward wickedness.

The meaning is: "Indeed, he has succeeded," but the lam was omitted because the speech became long, so its length became a substitute for it. Ibn al-Anbari said: its response is elided. The first: "Indeed, the soul has succeeded which Allah the Mighty and Majestic has purified," as said by Ibn Abbas, Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

The second: "Indeed, he has succeeded who purified his soul by obedience to Allah and righteous deeds," as said by Qatadah and Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Farra' said: it is related that "dassāhā" means "dassasahā," because the miser conceals his dwelling and his wealth. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: he buried his soul, that is, concealed it through immorality and disobedience. The exegetes said: suqyā means her drinking of the water, and the meaning is: do not interfere with the day of her drinking. ﴿But they denied him﴾ in his warning them of punishment for hamstringing her, ﴿and they hamstrung her﴾.
